nuggets.summary: When Soman pitched his friends-of-friends dating startup (Like Bright) to investors, they didn't push back on the product's quality — they pushed on growth curve shape, telling him a dating service needs lots of members and they wanted a curve that goes sharply up. He internalized this as a mandate and went and figured out how to grow a consumer app aggressively, effectively force-fitting growth tactics onto a product that hadn't yet proven it was good. The non-obvious lesson: investor pressure for a hockey-stick growth curve can push a founder to optimize distribution before the core experience is validated, which is backwards and can mask a weak product with vanity growth.
nuggets.quote: you tell a good story, clearly a dating service needs lots and lots of members to succeed. And I thought, yeah, you know, I want to offer that and I need to really nail this great user experience. And so I'm going to do both of those things. And they're like, great. But like really we kind of want to see a growth curve that goes [up]. And I thought, okay, then I guess I got to do that.

nuggets.summary: Soman's second startup (Reveal, an anonymous synchronous chat app) grew to roughly 1.5 million users and at one point hit 50,000 new users a day, almost entirely through Facebook as the acquisition channel. He never built out equally compelling alternative channels, so when Facebook's policy team cracked down on the dating vertical (which Reveal was classified under) and cut API access, the growth engine died almost overnight. His own read on the mistake: over-indexing on a single platform-owned channel for growth is a structural risk, not a strategy, because the platform will always act in its own interest over yours no matter how compliant you've been.
nuggets.quote: I over indexed on the Facebook channel as a way to grow rather than building out, you know, equally compelling alternatives, though that's honestly really, really hard to do. And so as a result, when they kind of cut off some API access from us early, which I get it, we weren't breaking any of their rules... they're a platform and they're going to control their platform. And that's a risk that I took.

nuggets.summary: After Like Bright failed, Soman's team wanted to test a completely different hypothesis (that people wanted synchronous, appearance-blind chat) but deliberately avoided repeating their earlier mistake of over-building a polished V1 before knowing if the core idea worked. Instead they threw up a deliberately ugly web experience with no reveal/photo functionality at all — just bare SMS-style chat with a stranger — and ran a single cheap Facebook ad campaign to drive two strangers into a conversation. The test validated the concept within about 45 minutes of live use, which is the concrete payoff of testing the riskiest assumption with the cheapest possible artifact instead of the full product vision.
nuggets.quote: we just said, okay, no, we're not going to do any of that stuff. We're going to throw up a crappy web experience, and we're going to put up some Facebook ads to try to bring two people in and just see if we can get them to talk to each other using the most simple and rudimentary UI imaginable. We didn't build in the ability to reveal information. It was literally just like SMS chat with a stranger.

nuggets.summary: When Reveal was acquired by Rhapsody and salaries doubled for much of the team, Soman expected the announcement of new (much higher) salaries to be the exciting moment for his employees. Instead, to a person, everyone's immediate response to hearing their new salary was to ask what they'd be working on next — not to celebrate the money. This flipped his assumption about what actually retains and motivates a team: people who stayed through a hard pivot were there for the mission, not the paycheck, and leading the conversation with salary instead of the next mission was, in his own assessment, the wrong instinct.
nuggets.quote: for a team that had worked so hard, that was super, super exciting. And they really impressed me and broke my heart a little bit because to a person, the response was, cool. What are we going to be working on? ... I think when I came in, I was a little bit of a blowhard. Like, check out your new salary instead of, you know, talking to them about the mission.

nuggets.summary: During the acquisition negotiation, Soman tried to keep every stakeholder (investors, team, his wife) happy by expressing more openness to different deal structures/options than he actually felt, rather than being as clear and firm about the outcome he believed was right as he had been about the company's mission. The result was that expressing flexibility invited a flood of alternative proposals — many of which he fundamentally didn't want to pursue — which slowed and muddied the process. His lesson: when you already know the right outcome by your own ethics, holding the line as tightly as you would on mission is faster and cleaner than staying "open" to please everyone.
nuggets.quote: I believe, I think, to some of those stakeholders outside of the team, I might have expressed a little bit too much flexibility about the different options that I'd be willing to consider... Guess what happens when you say that? You get a lot of other ideas... if anything, I think that's the time to hold the rudder even harder and be clearer about the thing you're trying to achieve for everybody involved.

nuggets.summary: Asked what operational advice he'd give a co-founder starting a new company, Soman's first answer was to pick exactly one key metric for the business — not a balanced scorecard. He explicitly rejects the common instinct to hedge with multiple metrics (e.g., growth balanced against net promoter score), arguing the value isn't in the metric itself but in the forcing function of the process of choosing just one, since that process is what surfaces what actually matters to the team; the single metric can change later, but there always has to be only one at a time, tracked obsessively and visible to everyone daily.
nuggets.quote: Find the one key metric that matters for your business... Like literally one. And don't give me some bullshit about, yeah, yeah, yeah, but it's growth, but it also has to be balanced with net promoter score... You might change what the one is, but you have to pick one. And you have to tell everybody what it is... And track the shit out of it. Just track it, track it, track it. Just track it at an embarrassing level.

nuggets.summary: Struggling to raise a first round for a dating startup with no track record in the category, Soman connected with Dr. Galen Buckwalter, the guy who wrote eHarmony's matching algorithm. Instead of preparing a pitch or a list of expert-testing questions, Soman researched him as a person, discovered he was also the lead singer of an all-therapist rock band, and spent the entire first call talking about music rather than the business. That personal, non-pitch conversation is what led Buckwalter to offer to advise and then invest — and Buckwalter's small check and a written endorsement then unlocked larger checks from other investors who had been on the fence, because his credibility functioned as third-party validation.
nuggets.quote: This is really the first time I'd had a human conversation with one of these people and not about the money. And he got so excited about that... he's like, I want to invest... I went back to these other investors... I got this guy who, you know, wrote the matching questions for eHarmony to invest. And he even wrote me a little blurbage... all these people suddenly said, Well, now we like you.

nuggets.summary: Soman describes routinely projecting inhuman, purely transactional motives onto investors early in his career — treating them as a category rather than as people. A friend snapped him out of this by pointing out, when Soman was anxiously overanalyzing whether he should accept an investor's invitation to his ranch, that the investor was just being a normal generous person, the same way Soman himself would be if he had an $11 million ranch. The reframe he took from it: investors and other stakeholders are just people, and treating them with basic transparency and humanness works better than trying to strategically manage them as instruments.
nuggets.quote: And Ben, in like very concise Ben fashion, he says, Nick, what would you do if you had an 11 million dollar ranch? ... And that was the point, is that in starting a company, you have to just recognize that these are people that you're dealing with. Treat them all as people.

nuggets.summary: Soman describes a specific, repeatable customer-research discipline his team runs weekly at the University of Washington: rather than asking prospective users "here's my idea, do you like it?" — which he calls a rookie mistake that never works — his team asks students to talk about their own lives and problems, and lets product opportunities surface from that. The discipline is maintained by team members (including alumni from the earlier Reveal team) running it every single week, treating negative feedback as the goal rather than something to fear, since being told an idea is flawed is the only way to improve it.
nuggets.quote: we go over to the University of Washington every week and we sit down with students to talk about what they're looking for and we don't make a couple rookie mistakes that we used to make like here's my idea do you like it? Never works. You have to just talk to them about their lives... we don't share our ideas because it's out of fear and maybe we'll be judged and like guess what I hope we get judged because then we can be told where the idea could be better.

nuggets.summary: Reflecting on being hospitalized and paralyzed for weeks with Guillain-Barré syndrome, Soman says the hardest part wasn't the physical pain of the illness itself — it was the sheer unstructured, empty time spent alone in a room, unable to move or be meaningfully present with people who loved him. This became the seed insight for the products he later built (a dating app, then an anonymous synchronous chat app): that loneliness is less about lacking people who care and more about the crushing volume of unfilled time, which reframes what a product trying to "cure loneliness" should actually be optimizing for.
nuggets.quote: It's not actually the pain of the illness. It's not the challenge of it. It's the interminable hours where you're laying in your room, and you know your friends love you, and it's not really about that. It's just about that there is so much time, it turns out, in the day when you can't move, when you can't be surrounded by people you love.

nuggets.summary: Reveal's core product mechanic let two strangers chat without seeing each other's photo or name unless both parties opted to reveal it after building trust through conversation. Soman cites a story a friend told him: he was chatting with a Muslim woman from Malaysia who asked to reveal photos only if he'd promise to remain friends afterward, because she'd learned that once people saw she was Muslim, some stopped wanting to be friends. This illustrates a non-obvious design principle: making identity-reveal optional and sequenced after connection can let people bypass the snap judgments (religion, appearance, etc.) that usually gate whether a relationship even starts.
nuggets.quote: one of my friends talked to a Muslim woman from Malaysia who said, you know, we can reveal our photos, but you have to promise we can still be friends after. And, you know, he said, sure, well, why? And she said, well, then you'll see that I'm a Muslim and maybe after that sometimes people don't want to be friends with me.

nuggets.summary: After his son was born, Soman assumed that pouring his own energy and attention directly onto the baby was what would keep the family okay. He instead learned the opposite worked better: when he shifted his focus to supporting his wife (his partner) first, his son ended up fine as a byproduct — what he calls the "transitive property." His generalized takeaway is that new parents often instinctively deprioritize the partnership in favor of direct child-focus, and that this doesn't actually work once you're also running a company, because you can't sustain three competing top priorities (spouse, kid, company) — the partnership needs to stay first.
nuggets.quote: I assumed that when my son was born, if I focused a lot of my energy and attention on him, then all would be right in the world. And I learned instead that as soon as I started focusing my energy and attention on Anna, by the transitive property, my son was okay.

nuggets.summary: Describing what he looks for in hires, Soman recounts the youngest person his company ever hired, Suzanne, a UW freshman who approached him saying she wanted to work with smart people — and, in the same breath, stated plainly that she expected to be paid for her work. He read that combination (confidence plus explicit self-advocacy about compensation, from someone with no track record) as a strong positive signal and says it turned into one of his best hiring decisions, suggesting that a candidate's willingness to state their own worth up front, even without credentials, is itself worth weighting heavily.
nuggets.quote: she said, I've heard you're smart and I'd like to work with you because I want to work with smart people... And she said, and I expect to be paid for my work. And I was just like, damn, okay, alright and we ended up hiring and it was one of the better decisions I've ever made.
